opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think compute is really the story of deep learning over the last decade or so. If you look back at when I was starting grad school, around the time AlexNet came out, we were training on a couple of GPUs for a week, and that felt like a lot. Since then the amount of compute we can throw at a single model has grown by many orders of magnitude, and every time it grows, the set of problems that become tractable changes.

Language models were a natural first beneficiary. Text is compact and already discretized, and there's a huge amount of it on the internet, so once you had enough compute you could just scale up a transformer and get remarkable capabilities. But I've always felt that language is a lossy, one-dimensional channel for describing the world. We live in a three-dimensional world that unfolds over time, governed by physics, geometry, and lighting. Representing and reasoning about that is fundamentally more data- and compute-hungry than modeling a sequence of tokens.

So for a long time world models, meaning systems that can perceive, generate, and reason about 3D space, were bottlenecked. You could do small-scale things: reconstruct a single object, render a scene with something like a NeRF after hours of per-scene optimization. But building a general model that understands and generates arbitrary 3D environments just wasn't feasible at the compute levels we had.

What's changing is that we're now at the point where the compute is there. The same scaling recipe that worked for language, big models, lots of data, simple objectives, can start to be applied to spatial data: images, video, multi-view captures, 3D representations. You see hints of this in video generation models, where scaling alone produces surprisingly coherent physical behavior and some 3D consistency. To me that's a signal that if you build the right representations and architectures with spatial structure in mind, and then scale them, you can get models that genuinely understand the 3D world rather than just mimicking pixels.

And the opportunity goes beyond research curiosity. Spatial intelligence underlies so much: robotics, design, games, AR and VR, simulation, creative tools. If you have a model that can take a few images or a text prompt and give you a consistent, explorable, interactive 3D world, that unlocks a whole range of applications. I think we're at an inflection point a lot like language was a few years ago, where compute has caught up with the ambition, and now it's a question of getting the data, the representations, and the engineering right.

r001.rationale: The response says compute has been “the story of deep learning” over the last decade and describes compute growing by many orders of magnitude.

r002.rationale: It identifies applying scaling to spatial data—images, video, multi-view captures, and 3D representations—as an opportunity enabled by growing compute.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way I think about this is that for the last decade or so, most of the compute in the field has been going toward one thing, which is language. And language is amazing, right — the internet gave us this enormous corpus of text, and it turned out that if you throw a lot of compute at next-token prediction on that corpus, you get these incredibly capable systems. That's been the dominant story.

But there's a lot of structure in the world that just isn't captured in text. Space, geometry, physics, how objects move, how light bounces off things — people don't write that down, because it's so obvious to us that we never bother. And so language models, even very big ones, have this kind of hole in their understanding of the physical world.

Now, if you look at where the compute curve is going, we're getting to a point where you can start throwing really serious compute at pixels. And pixels are a much denser signal than text. A single frame of video is way more bits than a sentence, and there's a basically unbounded amount of video and 3D data out there. Historically that was a problem — it was too expensive to learn from. The models you could afford to train on video were tiny compared to what you could train on text, so the results were underwhelming, and people sort of concluded that video was hard.

I think the growth in compute flips that around. The data was always there; what was missing was the ability to actually consume it at scale. So the opportunity for world models is that we're entering the regime where you can train a model to actually learn the structure of the physical world from observing it, the same way language models learned the structure of language from reading it. You get models that understand space, that understand that if I walk around this room the back of that chair is going to look a certain way, that understand consistency over time.

And the other thing I'd say is that this isn't just a research curiosity. Once you have models that understand 3D and physics, you unlock a bunch of applications that language alone can't touch — robotics, simulation, games, anything where you need to generate or reason about an environment rather than just describe it. So I see it less as world models competing with LLMs and more as, the compute has finally gotten cheap enough that we can go fill in the parts of intelligence that text was never going to give us.

r001.rationale: It describes compute scaling in language modeling as the dominant story over the last decade, but does not characterize the history of deep learning overall as a history of scaling compute.

r002.rationale: It says growing compute now makes it possible to train on pixels and other visual or 3D data at scale, learning the physical world.

astra-6.text:
I think the opportunity is that more compute lets us move beyond recognizing what’s in an image toward learning how the world changes over time. If you watch someone push an object, you don’t just see a sequence of pictures. You develop an expectation of how that object will move, what it might collide with, and what would happen if you pushed it differently. That’s the kind of capability we’d like these models to learn.

Video gives us a lot of data for that, but it’s expensive to model. You have to handle spatial detail, motion, and dependencies over time. As compute grows, we can start training models that capture more of that structure.

The really interesting step is making those models useful for taking actions. If a system can predict what might happen under different choices, it can use those predictions to plan. But generating a plausible video and making a prediction that’s reliable enough to act on are different things. More compute creates an opportunity to close that gap; it doesn’t automatically solve it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses how increasing compute could enable better world models, but it does not characterize deep learning’s history as a history of scaling compute.

r002.rationale: It connects growing compute to training models on video that capture spatial detail, motion, and change over time.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the opportunity is that we can start spending compute on learning how the world changes, rather than just recognizing what’s in an image. A world model needs to capture dynamics: if something moves, or an agent takes an action, what happens next? That’s a much richer problem, and it takes a lot of capacity and computation.

As more compute becomes available, you can train on longer sequences and build models that represent more of those interactions. Then the interesting question is whether you can use that model to try out possible actions—to predict their consequences before taking them. That creates a path from perception toward planning. Compute gives us room to explore that, although we still have to figure out the right learning objectives and how to tell whether a model has learned useful dynamics.

r001.rationale: The response discusses increasing compute as an opportunity, but does not characterize deep learning’s history as a history of scaling compute.

r002.rationale: It says available compute can be spent learning how the world changes, including interactions and action dynamics, directly identifying world modeling as a use for growing compute.
